title: Campus Rooms and Safety Rules
bigQuestion: How did schools and colleges take in fencing, wrestling, judo and sumo, and how did injuries push them to rewrite the rules?

story.title: A Trophy Case and a Rule Change
story.kicker: One school hallway holds a fencing sabre, a wrestling bracket and a new safety notice.
paragraphs: A trophy case stands in a college hallway. Behind the glass rests an old fencing sabre with a team photograph from the 1940s. Beside it hangs a wrestling bracket from a national tournament. A judo patch from a campus club is pinned in the corner.

Each object came to campus by a different road. Fencing came from European masters and city clubs. Wrestling grew into a school sport with its own national tournaments. Judo arrived with teachers from Japan's Kodokan in the early 1900s.

Taped to the glass is a newer paper. It is a safety notice about weigh-ins and head injuries. Rules like these were written after real harm to real students. Some changes came from colleges, some from state lawmakers and some from world federations.

The trophy case tells two stories at once. One is how schools welcomed arts from many places. The other is how schools changed those arts to protect the young people who practiced them. College weigh-in rules changed in 1998, and state concussion laws spread after 2009.
story.think: Why might a school's safety rules differ from the rules of the same art in a private club?

lessons.title: Guilds, Masters and the Mask
lessons.mainIdea: Fencing was first taught by licensed masters in guilds, and the wire mask of the late 1700s made practice safer.
reading: In 1487 the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick III granted a charter to a fencing *guild* called the Marxbrüder, based in Frankfurt. A guild was an organization of skilled workers that controlled training and licenses. Only guild members could call themselves masters and open schools. Other European cities had their own fencing guilds and licensed masters.

A fencing school was called a *salle*, from the French word for room. Masters taught paying pupils there with blunted swords. For centuries fencers practiced without face protection. Eye injuries and deaths in practice were a real risk. The master decided when a pupil was ready and signed the pupil's papers.

In the late 1700s French masters began using a *fencing mask* made of wire mesh. The French master La Boëssière is often credited with it. The mask let fencers practice at full speed with far less danger. It helped fencing move from a training for duels toward a sport.

words.d: an organization of skilled workers that controlled training and licenses in a trade
a fencing school or training room, from the French word for room
a wire mesh face guard that came into use in France in the late 1700s

look.title: Two Licenses
look.text: A fencing master in Frankfurt in 1500 shows a guild certificate before he may open a school. A college fencing coach in 1950 shows a teaching contract from the college and a membership card in a national fencing league.
look.prompt: Who gave each teacher the right to teach? What changed about who controls the art?

check.why: Emperor Frederick III chartered the Marxbrüder guild in 1487.

check.q: What is a salle?
choices: a fencing school or training room
check.why: Salle comes from the French word for room and names a fencing school.

check.q: How did the wire mask change fencing?
choices: It let fencers practice at full speed with far less danger
It made fencing an Olympic sport in 1487
check.why: The mask made practice much safer and helped fencing become a sport.

lessons.title: Clubs and Colleges in America
lessons.mainIdea: American fencing gained a national league in 1891, a college association in 1894 and an NCAA championship in 1941.
reading: In 1891 American fencers founded the *Amateur Fencers League of America*, or AFLA. It held national championships and set rules for amateur fencing. In 1981 it became the United States Fencing Association. Today the body is called USA Fencing. It later joined the FIE, the world fencing federation founded in Paris in 1913.

Colleges formed their own group in 1894, the *Intercollegiate Fencing Association*. Eastern universities held team meets under its rules. Fencing grew as a college sport before many campuses had wrestling or basketball teams. College fencers competed with the three weapons: foil, épée and sabre.

The *NCAA*, the National Collegiate Athletic Association, held its first fencing championships in 1941. Fencing now had a national college title, a rule book and a place on the athletic budget. The old master and pupil bond moved into a system of coaches, teams and seasons.

words.d: the U.S. fencing body founded in 1891, now called USA Fencing
a college fencing group founded in 1894
the National Collegiate Athletic Association, which runs many U.S. college championships

look.title: Three Weapons, One Team
look.text: A 1940s college fencing team lists three squads: foil, épée and sabre. Each squad has its own fencers. The team score adds up bouts from all three weapons. The coach, not a guild, decides who fences.
look.prompt: How is a college team different from a master's salle with private pupils?

check.q: When was the Amateur Fencers League of America founded?
check.why: The AFLA began in 1891; the college association came in 1894.

check.q: What happened in 1941?
choices: The NCAA held its first fencing championships
check.why: The first NCAA fencing championships took place in 1941.

check.q: What is USA Fencing today?
choices: the national body that grew from the AFLA
check.why: The AFLA became the United States Fencing Association in 1981 and is now USA Fencing.

lessons.title: Women Take the Strip
lessons.mainIdea: Women fenced in the Olympics from 1924 and in their own college association from 1929, but waited until 1982 for an NCAA title.
reading: Women first fenced in the Olympic Games in 1924 in Paris, in a single event with the foil. Other weapons stayed closed to women at the Olympics for decades. Women's épée joined the Games in 1996, and women's sabre in 2004. Each opening came from a vote of the governing bodies.

In American colleges, women formed the *National Intercollegiate Women's Fencing Association* in 1929. It ran women's college championships for more than fifty years. Women's colleges and coeducational universities in the East sent teams to its meets. The group kept women's fencing alive while men's college sport grew under the NCAA.

The NCAA added a women's fencing championship in 1982, ten years after Title IX. In 1990 the NCAA combined the men's and women's events into one team championship. Men and women now score for the same *team title*. Fencing is one of the few NCAA sports that does this.

words.d: a light fencing weapon; the first weapon women fenced in the Olympics, in 1924
a women's college fencing group founded in 1929
a championship won by a whole team's combined score

check.q: Which weapon did women fence first at the Olympics?
check.why: Foil came in 1924; épée followed in 1996 and sabre in 2004.

lessons.title: A Federation Born in Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: In 1920 five Midwestern state associations, including Illinois, met in Chicago to form the group that now writes national high school rules.
reading: On May 14, 1920, leaders of five state high school associations met in Chicago. They came from Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Michigan and Wisconsin. They formed the Midwest Federation of State High School Athletic Associations. Within a few years it became a national body.

Today it is the *National Federation of State High School Associations*, or NFHS. It writes playing rules for many high school sports, including wrestling. A state *association*, like the IHSA in Illinois, runs the tournaments and follows or adapts those rules. Colleges follow separate NCAA rules.

The federation was formed partly to stop colleges and private promoters from running high school contests. The founders wanted school leaders to control school sports. That choice shaped wrestling in America. It became a school sport run by educators, with *eligibility* rules about grades, age and enrollment.

words.w: National Federation of State High School Associations
words.d: the NFHS, founded in Chicago in 1920, which writes national high school playing rules
a group of members, such as the schools of one state, that runs its own contests
the rules about who is allowed to compete, such as grades, age and enrollment

check.why: Leaders of five state associations met in Chicago on May 14, 1920.

check.why: The NFHS writes high school rules; the NCAA handles colleges.

check.q: What are eligibility rules?
choices: rules about who is allowed to compete
check.why: Eligibility rules cover who may compete, such as grades, age and enrollment.

lessons.title: Gable's Iowa Room
lessons.mainIdea: Dan Gable's career as a college wrestler, Olympic champion and Iowa coach shows how American wrestling grew inside universities.
reading: Dan Gable grew up in Waterloo, Iowa, and wrestled for Iowa State University. He lost only one college match, the 1970 NCAA final, to Larry Owings of Washington. At the 1972 Olympics in Munich he won a gold medal in freestyle wrestling. Reports from the Games note that no opponent scored a point on him.

In 1976 Gable became head *coach* at the University of Iowa. His teams won 15 NCAA team titles before he retired from coaching in 1997. Iowa City became a center of college wrestling. Crowds filled the university arena for home meets. Iowa's teams also won 21 Big Ten titles under Gable.

Gable's story shows how the United States built wrestling through schools and colleges, not through private clubs. College programs produced many American Olympic *freestyle* wrestlers. American colleges use their own *folkstyle* rules, which differ from the Olympic freestyle rules. Athletes switch between the two rule books.

words.d: the leader who trains and manages a school or college team
one of the two Olympic styles of wrestling
the style of wrestling used in U.S. high schools and colleges, with its own rules

check.why: Gable won freestyle gold at the 1972 Munich Olympics.

choices: a style used only in the Army

check.why: Folkstyle is the American school and college style, separate from Olympic freestyle.

check.q: How many NCAA team titles did Gable's Iowa teams win?
check.why: Iowa won 15 NCAA team titles under Gable from 1976 to 1997.

sections.title: Judo and Sumo in School Rooms

lessons.title: A Judo Teacher at the White House
lessons.mainIdea: Yamashita Yoshitsugu of the Kodokan taught judo to President Theodore Roosevelt in 1904 and then at the U.S. Naval Academy.
reading: Yamashita Yoshitsugu was one of the first students of Kanō Jigorō at the *Kodokan*, the judo school in Tokyo. He came to the United States in 1903. In 1904 President Theodore Roosevelt took judo lessons from him at the White House. Roosevelt wrote about the lessons in letters.

Yamashita then taught judo at the *U.S. Naval Academy* in Annapolis, Maryland, for a time around 1905. It was one of the first times an American school gave judo a place in its training. His wife, Yamashita Fude, is recorded as teaching judo to American women during their stay. The couple returned to Japan in 1907.

In 1935, after his death, the Kodokan made Yamashita its first tenth *dan*, its highest rank. His years in America show judo arriving on campus through one teacher, not through a national program. The art came with a Kodokan lineage, but the Naval Academy used it as military training.

words.d: the judo school Kanō Jigorō founded in Tokyo in 1882
the college in Annapolis, Maryland, that trains officers for the Navy
a rank in judo and other Japanese arts; tenth dan is the highest

look.title: One Teacher, Two Rooms
look.text: In 1904 Yamashita teaches the President in a room at the White House. In 1905 he teaches midshipmen at a naval college. In the first room judo is a private study. In the second it is part of officer training.
look.prompt: What changes about judo when it moves from a private lesson to a military college?

check.why: Theodore Roosevelt studied with Yamashita at the White House in 1904.

check.why: Kanō founded the Kodokan in Tokyo in 1882.

check.q: What rank did the Kodokan give Yamashita in 1935?
choices: a black belt for teaching women
check.why: Yamashita became the Kodokan's first tenth dan in 1935.

lessons.title: Sumo's College Door
lessons.mainIdea: In Japan, school and university sumo clubs became a path into professional sumo, as the career of Wajima shows.
reading: Professional sumo in Japan is run by the *Japan Sumo Association*. Wrestlers live and train in stables, called heya, under a stablemaster. Many enter as teenagers straight from middle school. Others first wrestle in high school and university clubs, which run their own amateur tournaments.

Wajima Hiroshi wrestled for Nihon University in Tokyo and won major student titles. He entered professional sumo in 1970. Because of his *amateur* record, he was allowed to start in a higher division instead of the lowest. He reached the top rank of *yokozuna* in 1973.

Wajima won 14 top-division championships. His path showed that a university club could feed the professional sport. Today many top wrestlers come from college sumo. A school room and a professional stable now form two stages of one career. Nihon University and other schools are known for sending wrestlers into the top division.

words.d: the body that runs professional sumo in Japan
an athlete who competes without being paid, such as a college wrestler
the highest rank in professional sumo

look.title: Two Roads to a Stable
look.text: One wrestler joins a professional stable at 15, right after middle school, and starts in the lowest division. Another wrestles four years for a university club, wins a national student title, and enters the professional sport at 22 in a higher division.
look.prompt: What does each road give a wrestler? Why might the professional body reward a college record?

check.why: Wajima wrestled for Nihon University in Tokyo.

check.q: What is a yokozuna?

check.why: Strong amateur results let college wrestlers enter at a higher division.

lessons.title: Three Deaths in 1997
lessons.mainIdea: After three college wrestlers died while cutting weight in late 1997, the NCAA rewrote its weight rules in 1998.
reading: Wrestlers compete in *weight classes*, so each athlete faces someone of about the same weight. Many wrestlers tried to lose weight fast before weigh-ins to compete in a lower class. This practice is called *cutting weight*. It often meant going without water in hot rooms.

Between November and December 1997, three college wrestlers died while cutting weight. They were Billy Saylor of Campbell University in North Carolina, Joseph LaRosa of the University of Wisconsin-La Crosse and Jeff Reese of the University of Michigan. Each died within weeks of the others. Their deaths shocked schools and families.

In 1998 the NCAA changed its rules. It banned rubber suits and saunas for losing weight and moved *weigh-ins* closer to the start of competition. Later it set a lowest allowed weight for each wrestler, based on a body-fat test. High school associations adopted similar weight plans in the years that followed.

words.d: a group of athletes of about the same body weight who compete against each other
losing weight fast before a weigh-in to compete in a lower class
the official check of an athlete's weight before competition

look.title: Before and After 1998
look.text: Before 1998, a college wrestler could weigh in the day before a meet, after days in a rubber suit. After 1998, rubber suits and saunas were banned for losing weight, and the weigh-in moved close to the first match.
look.prompt: How does moving the weigh-in closer to the match change what a wrestler has reason to do?

check.q: What is cutting weight?
choices: losing weight fast before a weigh-in
check.why: Cutting weight means losing weight fast to compete in a lower class.

check.q: What did the NCAA do in 1998?
choices: banned rubber suits and saunas and moved weigh-ins closer to matches
check.why: The 1998 rules targeted the practices tied to the three deaths.

check.q: When did the three college wrestlers die?
check.why: All three died within weeks of each other in late 1997.

lessons.title: The Lystedt Law
lessons.mainIdea: Washington State's 2009 Lystedt Law set the model for school concussion laws that every state later passed.
reading: In 2006 Zackery Lystedt, a 13-year-old football player in Maple Valley, Washington, suffered a brain injury. He had returned to a game after a blow to the head. The injury left him with lasting disabilities. His family worked with doctors and lawmakers to change the rules.

In 2009 Washington passed the *Lystedt Law*. It had three main parts. Schools must teach athletes, parents and coaches about *concussion*, a brain injury caused by a blow or jolt. An athlete who may have one must be removed from play, and may return only with written *clearance* from a licensed health care provider.

Other states copied the model, and by 2014 every state had a youth concussion law. The laws cover wrestling, judo clubs in schools and other contact sports, not only football. Illinois passed its own school concussion laws. A single injury in one state changed rules in gyms across the country.

words.d: the 2009 Washington State law that set rules for concussions in youth sports
a brain injury caused by a blow or jolt to the head or body
written permission from a licensed health care provider to return to play

lessons.title: Headgear Comes Off
lessons.mainIdea: In 2013 amateur boxing's world body removed headgear for elite men, showing that safety rules can change direction.
reading: Olympic boxers wore *headgear*, padded head guards, from 1984 on. Many people assumed headgear made the sport safer. In 2013 the world amateur boxing body, then called AIBA, removed headgear for elite men's bouts. Women and youth boxers kept it. The Olympic rule for men had lasted nearly thirty years.

AIBA said its own medical data supported the change. Some doctors disagreed and asked for more research. The same year AIBA adopted the ten-point must *scoring system*, the system used in professional boxing. Men boxed without headgear at the 2016 Olympics in Rio de Janeiro.

The change shows that safety rules are claims that can be tested and argued. A school, a college and a world *federation* may reach different answers about the same equipment. USA Boxing kept headgear for youth events. Each body writes rules for its own athletes.

words.d: a padded guard worn on the head in some combat sports
the method judges use to decide who wins a bout
an organization that joins national groups to run a sport and write its rules

look.prompt: Why might different bodies reach different decisions about the same piece of equipment?

check.q: What is a federation?
choices: an organization that joins national groups to run a sport
check.why: A federation joins national groups and writes the sport's rules.
